rss_3_1788553900.title: Tropical cyclones could be predicted with an extra day’s warning, thanks to an AI model
rss_3_1788553900.text:
Tropical cyclones — also called typhoons or hurricanes, depending on where they occur — are a major cause of deaths worldwide, and inflict considerable damage on property and infrastructure. The formation and evolution of these rapidly rotating weather systems are driven by effects on a range of scales, which makes it incredibly challenging to forecast them accurately using conventional models. Now, writing in Nature, Alet et al.1 introduce WeatherNext Cyclones (WN-C), an artificial-intelligence model that can produce two-week forecasts of unfolding tropical cyclones.

rss_4_1788553901.title: Ada Yonath obituary: Crystallographer who overcame ‘impossible’ challenge of mapping the ribosome
rss_4_1788553901.text:
Credit: Micheline Pelletier/Corbis/Getty

Grit and determination feature in most scientific careers, but the Israeli structural biologist Ada Yonath surmounted more obstacles than most. Yonath was the first to grow crystals suitable for X-ray analysis that would reveal the structure of the ribosome — a macromolecular complex that functions as a factory for proteins in living cells and is fundamental to implementing the genetic instructions to make a living organism. For this work, she won a share of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Yonath was the fourth of eight women ever to win the chemistry Nobel, and the first since Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin, 45 years previously. But she never saw her gender as important, saying, “I am a scientist, not male or female. A scientist.”

Yonath, who has died aged 87, explored the interaction of antibiotics that were known to exert their effects through binding to bacterial ribosomes. These studies not only revealed how such compounds disrupt ribosomal function, but also shed light on antibiotic resistance and opened up the possibility of designing new drugs.

Making samples one billion times bigger lets simple microscopes pinpoint amino acids

Born Ada Lifshitz in Jerusalem to an impoverished Orthodox Jewish family, Yonath lost her father when she was 11 years old. Her parents had little education themselves, but they encouraged her insatiable curiosity. Despite having to take evening and weekend jobs to support her family, she graduated from Beit Hakerem (now Hebrew University Secondary School), an academically rigorous secular institution, and completed undergraduate and master’s degrees at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She obtained a doctorate in structural biology at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Tel Aviv, Israel, working on the protein collagen.

After completing postdocs at the Mellon Institute (a forerunner of Carnegie Mellon University) in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania and at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, she returned to the Weizmann Institute in 1970 to set up Israel’s first biological crystallography laboratory. Although she initially studied individual proteins, she conceived the idea of working out the structure of the ribosome.

It was an impossible task with the technology available at the time, and she was widely ridiculed. The ribosome is composed of a large and a small subunit, which together comprise a complex of protein and ribosomal RNA amounting to some hundreds of thousands of atoms — more than ten times larger than any molecule solved previously.

How to win a Nobel prize: what kind of scientist scoops medals?

Furthermore, X-ray crystallography requires a crystal — and no one had so far crystallized the large, asymmetric and flexible ribosome. Yonath went to West Germany to work at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics in West Berlin, with its director Heinz-Günther Wittmann, whose lab was devoted to the study of ribosomes from many different species. With his support and contributions from his colleagues, Yonath was able to tackle a challenge that would take decades.

rss_5_1788553903.title: Revealed: inside the US military's plan to tap huge sums from the NIH
rss_5_1788553903.text:
Scientists work in a laboratory at the National Institutes of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, which could lose research projects to the US Department of Defense.Credit: NIAID

The US National Institutes of Health (NIH) is seeking to redirect research projects worth hundreds of millions of dollars from its infectious-diseases institute to military biodefence programmes at the US Department of Defense (DOD), according to two NIH employees.

They confirmed to Nature that the NIH and the DOD, also called the Department of War, have signed an agreement for the arrangement. The NIH is now identifying projects it would transfer to the DOD and aims to complete the agreement by the end of September, when the fiscal year ends and some funds expire, according to a third NIH employee who is a senior official at the agency. (The employees spoke on the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the press.)

An NIH spokesperson says, “This partnership will only take place on a project-by-project basis, and all research will be within the scope of NIH’s mission. There is no blanket transfer of funds”.

Exclusive: NIH ousts infectious-disease leaders as COVID scientists face US charges

The senior NIH official said the new arrangement would untangle civilian public-health initiatives from defence priorities. “We’re trying to get research that’s more Department of War-related back to Department of War,” the official said. “When the public hears that NIAID funds biodefence, they think we’re developing bioweapons, and we’re trying to get out of that business.”

Federal law does allow agreements between US agencies to share funding in some circumstances, says Samuel Bagenstos, who until December 2025 was the top lawyer for the NIH’s parent agency, the Department of Health and Human Services. But “what’s not appropriate or legal is saying, ‘Look, DOD needs money, NIH has money, we’re going to take money and send it to the DOD,’” he says. If the administration is using NIH resources to cover military budget shortfalls, “that would be illegal, because that would be using funding not to serve the purposes of NIH, but to serve the purposes of DOD.”

The agreement would establish a pathway to move funding out of the NIH’s National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), the country’s premier infectious-disease research institute, to support defence initiatives and will last 10 years, according to the three sources. The full agreement has not yet been finalized, the sources say.

Biosecurity researchers warn that shifting biomedical research to the military threatens the transparency and clinical translation that define NIH-funded work. “The Department of Defense is just not set up to deliver the scientific innovations we have come to expect and rely on from NIH,” says Gigi Gronvall, a biosecurity specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health in Baltimore, Maryland.

Bureaucratic churn

The agreement comes as the administration of US president Donald Trump has ousted eight of ten of the NIAID’s top officials and reoriented NIAID away from research that anticipates emerging viral threats and toward basic immunology and domestic chronic illnesses. Nature reported in February that NIAID staff had been instructed to scrub the terms “biodefense” and “pandemic preparedness” from the institute’s website.

The NIAID’s biodefence portfolio includes research aimed at developing vaccines and treatments for weaponized pathogens such as anthrax, smallpox and plague, as well as medical countermeasures to protect against nerve agents and radiation sickness from nuclear detonations.

Saskia Popescu, an infectious-disease epidemiologist at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, says that although biodefence requires military and civilian coordination, moving work away from NIAID risks fragmenting national preparedness for emergencies such as pandemics.

NIH director Jay Bhattacharya defended the arrangement between the two agencies. “Far from siphoning money away from research, this partnership between @NIH and @Dept ofWar focuses on research projects that will drive discoveries to improve the health of American citizens and members of the military,” Bhattacharya wrote in a post on social media platform X.

Operation Prevailing Edge

The reallocation was initiated by NIH leadership, but Robert Kadlec, assistant secretary of defense for nuclear deterrence, chemical and biological defense policy and programs, has been pushing to finalize the deal under a broader biodefence initiative dubbed “Operation Prevailing Edge”, according to two of the three NIH employees.

rss_6_1788553905.title: Buried underpants and a new definition of kissing win 2026 Ig Nobel prizes
rss_6_1788553905.text:
Researchers found that land use is a key factor in the decomposition of underwear, more so than other soil characteristics.Credit: Gabriela Brändle/Agroscope

The recognition and prestige of a Nobel prize for groundbreaking work comes with a gold medal and the equivalent of about US$1 million. The parody version, an Ig Nobel prize, devised to celebrate research that makes people laugh, and then think, might not deliver on the cash front, but it does bring considerable renown.

This year’s Ig Nobel prizes were awarded on 3 September at a ceremony in Zurich, Switzerland. They include a biomechanics prize for creating a precise definition of kissing, which works across species and excludes the transfer of food during the act1, a physics award that aims to please with experiments to design a splash-free urinal2 and a soil-science award for investigating what happens if you bury and then dig up 1,000 pairs of underwear3 (see ‘The 2026 Ig Nobel prizewinners in full’).

“I hope that, as well as finding the research amusing, people will come away thinking a little differently about our place in the animal kingdom,” says Matilda Brindle, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Oxford, UK, who was a co-author of the kissing study. “My jaw hit the floor when I got the phone call. It’s certainly one of my proudest life achievements.”

Smooching with Neanderthals

Brindle’s team steamily defined kissing as a “non-agonistic interaction involving directed, intraspecific, oral–oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer”. According to this definition, polar bears, some birds and even ants kiss. What’s more, not only do other primates also snog each other, but the behaviour traces back around 21.5 million years to the ancestor of all the large apes, found the team. This means that ancient Homo sapiens would probably have been smooching Neanderthals.

“We’ve shown that animals kiss and when it could have evolved in the primates; the obvious next step is understanding why. If this award helps spark more curiosity about this sort of question, then that’s a pretty wonderful outcome,” says Brindle.

Levitating frogs

Previous winners of Ig Nobel prizes have included researchers who studied the preferred pizza toppings of rainbow lizards (Agama agama) in Togo4, the levitation of live frogs using magnets5 and research showing that London taxi drivers have particularly large hippocampi in their brains6.

In the prize’s early days — it was launched in 1991 by Marc Abrahams, editor of the satirical magazine Annals of Improbable Research — receiving an Ig Nobel prize was deemed insulting by some, but now many researchers see the awards as a great career boost.

How a silly science prize changed my career

“The visibility they bring is enormous. It exposes research to audiences that would never otherwise encounter it,” says Changhong Cao, a mechanical engineer at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, who is part of the team that won this year’s technology prize for showing that a mosquito’s mouthparts can be repurposed as a nozzle for high-resolution, low-cost 3D printing7.

Cao says that the work shows that even things that people find unpleasant can turn out to be useful — sometimes in the most unexpected way.

Another example of unpalatable items coming in handy is the work of Franz Bender and Marcel van der Heijden at the University of Zurich, who were the researchers responsible for the underwear-burial study. They enlisted community scientists from more than 25 nations to bury the garments and dig them up two months later, which provided insight into how biologically active the soil was.

The 2026 Ig Nobel prizewinners in full BIOMECHANICS Matilda Brindle, Catherine Talbot and Stuart West, for devising a precise definition of kissing1. ECONOMICS Paul Piff, Daniel Stancato, Stéphane Côté, Rodolfo Mendoza-Denton and Dacher Keltner, for amassing evidence that wealthy people are more likely to engage in unethical behavior than are people with lower incomes8. CHEMISTRY Sanchari Banerjee, Nathan Coussens, François-Xavier Gallat, Nitish Sathyanarayanan, Jandhyam Srikanth, Koichiro Yagi, James Gray, Stephen Tobe, Barbara Stay, Leonard Chavas and Subramanian Ramaswamy, for discovering that milk proteins from cockroaches that give birth to live young contain three times as much energy as milk proteins from cows9. MEDICINE The late Tokuji Unno, for the 1977 study called ‘How to Blow the Nose — An Aerodynamic Study of the Nose Blowing’10. BIOLOGY João Miguel Alves-Nunes, Adriano Fellone, Selma Maria Almeida-Santos, Carlos Roberto de Medeiros, Ivan Sazima and Otavio Augusto Vuolo Marques, for gently stepping on various parts of snakes to try to learn what induces a venomous snake to bite a human11. PHYSICS Randy Hurd, Zhao Pan, Tadd Truscott and Kaveeshan Thurairajah, for theoretical and experimental attempts to design a splash-free urinal2. TECHNOLOGY Justin Puma, Zhen Yang, Evan Johnston, Zixin Zhang, Xiaoyi Lan, Lingzhi Zhang, Hongyu Hou, Zixin He, Ali Afify, Megan Creighton, Jianyu Li and Changhong Cao, for pioneering the use of mosquito proboscises as high-resolution 3D printing nozzles, a process called necroprinting7. OLFACTION Ilona Croy, Tomasz Frackowiak, Thomas Hummel and Agnieszka Sorokowska, for collecting evidence that babies smell great to their parents, but teenagers do not12. PEACE Jaimie Arona Krems, Rebecka Hahnel-Peeters, Laureon Merrie, Keelah Williams and Daniel Sznycer, for documenting that people value friends who are mean to those that they dislike13. SOIL SCIENCE Franz Bender, Marcel van der Heijden, Atlant Bieri and Pia Viviani, for burying 1,000 pairs of underwear in more than 25 nations and digging them up two months later3.

Like candy from a baby

Other awards this year include the physics prize for a team that experimentally validated what makes fluid splash back from urinals and suggested redesigns that could cut the spray to just 1.4% of what is commonly experienced.

rss_7_1788553906.title: Bunsen burners’ reputation for sterilizing workplaces flames out
rss_7_1788553906.text:
The Bunsen burner’s future in modern microbiology labs is flickering, some scientists say. Credit: Alfonso Fabio Iozzino/Alamy

The Bunsen burner, a workhorse of biology and chemistry labs around the world for decades, might have been getting more credit than it deserves.

Many scientists have long relied on Bunsen burners to decontaminate airspace and surfaces in labs. The burners’ flames were thought to create convection currents that carry microbe-containing particles away from the lab bench. Now, a study has found not only that the devices are ineffective at cleansing workspaces of bacteria-laden particles, but that they can even make contamination worse.

The work was published in August in Microbiology Spectrum1.

Even before the study came out, biologists had divided opinions about Bunsen burners, says Hannah Gavin, a microbiologist at Providence College in Rhode Island and a co-author of the paper. Some researchers swore by the burners’ ability to sterilize research spaces, but others had doubts. The study could fuel debate about whether this low-tech device still has a place in the modern laboratory. It could even be the “nail in the coffin” for the burners’ use in biology labs, says Amir Mitchell, a systems biologist at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School in Worcester.

Tradition debunked

Researchers began using Bunsen burners almost two centuries ago. Despite the apparatus’s long history, Gavin could find no experimental evidence in the scientific literature that Bunsen burners decontaminate their surroundings. That information void “allowed for the propagation of all these hypotheses, theories, lore, mythology around the Bunsen burner”, she says.

To find out once and for all whether the burners can shoo away errant bacteria, Gavin and her colleagues grew a strain of Gordonia rubripertincta, a bright orange bacterium that is easy to spot on Petri dishes and does not commonly contaminate labs. In their experiments, the authors aimed to represent the numerous sources of unwanted bacteria — from vacuum cleaners stirring up bacteria-laden dust to scientists’ sneezes and shed skin cells.

Your lab pollutes: here’s how to stop it

To do so, Gavin and her team ran trials in which they seeded the air above lab benches with bacteria by either spraying liquid containing G. rubripertincta in the air or shaking dry towels laced with the bacteria. Immediately after deliberately contaminating the workspace, the researchers turned on a Bunsen burner and opened a Petri dish next to it; they also opened a dish next to an inactive burner in a paired contaminated workspace, beyond the active flame’s reach. They left the dishes open to give bacteria a chance to settle on the dishes’ surfaces, before closing them again.

The researchers varied the size of the burner, the levels of bacterial contamination and other experimental conditions. They found that in almost every trial, the level of bacteria in the dish next to the active Bunsen burner was equal to or higher than the level in the dish next to the inactive burner. The only experiment in which fewer bacteria settled in the active burner’s dish was one in which the amount of bacteria launched into the air was “orders of magnitude higher”, Gavin says, than would be found in most modern labs.

rss_8_1788553908.title: Ketone homologation via palladium-catalysed decarboxylative rearrangement
rss_8_1788553908.text: The decarboxylative semi-pinacol rearrangement of β-hydroxy carboxylic acids under electrochemical oxidation conditions was first reported in 19601. However, its further development has remained limited owing to stepwise radical and carbocationic pathways that induce side reactions and result in the loss of stereochemical information at the α-carbon. Herein, we demonstrate that this transformation can instead be realized through a concerted mechanism under Pd(II)/Pd(IV) catalysis. The reaction proceeds via the formation of a six-membered Pd(IV) chelate, which undergoes fragmentation accompanied by β-to-α carbon migration and carbon dioxide extrusion, with Pd(IV) serving as the redox center. This closed-shell pathway enables precise stereochemical control: the migrating carbon retains its absolute configuration, while the α-stereocenter undergoes inversion. For unsymmetrical ketones, the reaction displays markedly higher migrating-group selectivity than the classical Tiffeneau–Demjanov2 and Büchner–Curtius–Schlotterbeck reactions3. Broadly applicable to cyclic and acyclic ketones and aldehydes, this method avoids hazardous diazo reagents. Its utility is illustrated by a concise total synthesis of (+)-rupestine D, where the rearrangement serves as a key carbon-skeleton-editing step.

rss_9_1788553909.title: Immune therapy engineered inside the body eases multiple sclerosis
rss_9_1788553909.text:
Credit: Keith Chambers/SPL

Symptoms for 16 people with multiple sclerosis or other autoimmune conditions improved after receiving a treatment that produced disease-fighting immune cells inside their bodies, according to results1 from a small clinical trial. Researchers say the results are exciting but the treatment needs to be tested in more people.

The latest trial, published this week in The New England Journal of Medicine, used a modified virus to transfer genetic instructions for making chimaeric antigen receptors (CARs) on participants’ immune cells, known as T cells. The CAR T cells target autoantibodies expressed by B cells, another type of immune cell, which attack the body’s own healthy tissue in people with autoimmune diseases.

“This is a very exciting proof-of-concept study” for in vivo CAR-T-cell therapy, which is made inside the body, says David Simon, a clinician-researcher at the Charité — University Medicine Berlin. In vivo therapy is cheaper and faster to produce than is conventional CAR-T-cell therapies that are made in a laboratory, he adds.

Conventionally, CAR-T-cell therapies involve collecting T cells from a person’s blood and editing them in the lab to produce CARs. The tweaked cells are then reintroduced to the body. Ex vivo CAR-T-cell therapies are used to treat blood cancers, and clinical trials are under way to test them against autoimmune diseases such as lupus.

Developing an in vivo CAR-T treatment for any disease is “a big achievement”, says Bing Du, an immunologist at East China Normal University in Shanghai. The results are good and comparable with those for ex vivo CAR-T-cell therapy, he says.

Dai-Shi Tian, one of the trial’s lead investigators, says the team was encouraged by the results. “The responses are promising signals, but they are not yet definitive evidence of efficacy or permanent restoration of immune tolerance,” says Tian, a neurologist at Tongji Medical College at Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan, China.

Immune reset

The trial involved people with multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune conditions, including those that cause weakness or inflammation of a person’s muscles, or in which the immune system attacks the brain, spinal cord and eyes. The participants received a single injection of the viral cells into their bloodstream and were monitored for about six months.

The team used a virus called a lentivirus, designed by biotechnology company Shenzhen Genocury Biotech in China. Last year, another CAR-T-cell therapy using a lentivirus was shown to effectively treat blood cancer2.

The team reported that, following treatment, the participants generated more CAR T cells over time. These helped to deplete the number of B cells and levels of autoantibodies that attack healthy tissue. The team says the participants’ replacement B cells did not produce such autoantibodies, suggesting that their immune systems had been reset. The people with multiple sclerosis showed improved motor and cognitive function, as well as reductions in fatigue. Those with other conditions affecting their muscles showed improved scores for muscle strength and decreased inflammation.

rss_10_1788553911.title: Magic-mushroom compound blocks a severe side effect of chemotherapy in mice
rss_10_1788553911.text:
Studies in mice suggest that psilocybin, one of the psychoactive compounds in magic mushrooms, could prevent the chemotherapy side effect called neuropathy.Credit: Victor de Schwanberg/SPL

For many cancer survivors, the triumph of remission is undercut by a debilitating side effect: hands and feet that feel as though they are constantly burning, prickling with needles or encased in ice. Now, researchers studying this condition, called neuropathy, in mice have identified an unexpected defence against it: psilocybin, the psychoactive compound found in magic mushrooms.

Just two doses of psilocybin administered before chemotherapy completely prevented mice from developing neuropathy. The condition affects as many as 60% of people treated with platinum-based cancer drugs, which are widely used to treat tumours of the ovaries and lungs, for example. The results, published today in Science, offer evidence that psilocybin could help to protect nerve fibres before chemotherapy causes lasting injury1 — which current approaches can’t effectively prevent or treat.

“This study pushes the needle beyond the canonical indications of psychedelics like depression, addiction, anxiety, PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder],” says study co-author Moran Amit, a surgical oncologist at the MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, Texas. “For the first time, we’re looking at pain,” he says. “And we’re actually showing a really significant efficacy not in treating that, but in preventing that.”

Neuron starvation

Platinum-based cancer drugs and other chemotherapies cause neuropathy by damaging some of the information-gathering ‘sensory’ neurons that extend into the skin’s outer layers. Energy-producing organelles called mitochondria travel long distances through these neurons to the cells’ tips in the skin, but some chemotherapies can disrupt that process. Depleted of energy, the neurons’ tips degenerate, dulling tactile sensation and sparking chronic pain.

Faulty mitochondria cause deadly diseases: fixing them is about to get a lot easier

To test whether psilocybin could ward off that breakdown, the researchers gave mice two doses of the compound before the animals received each of six rounds of chemotherapy over eight months.

In untreated animals, chemotherapy caused pain hypersensitivity, dulled their ability to feel sensations in their paws and led sensory-nerve fibres in the skin to wither. But psilocybin pre-treatment preserved normal paw sensation and nerve endings without diminishing the chemotherapy’s ability to shrink tumours, the authors found.

The authors’ strategy of administering psilocybin to prevent neuropathy, rather than trying to undo damage, is a “clever treatment approach”, says Joe Cichon, a neuroanaesthesiologist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

No trip needed

The authors found that psilocybin stops nerve decay by activating specific receptors on sensory nerve fibres across the animals’ skin. Turning on these receptors triggers a series of reactions that eventually enlist motor proteins to keep mitochondria moving along the neurons. “That’s quite surprising — I wouldn’t have expected psilocybin to regulate mitochondrial movement,” Cichon says.

These neuroprotective effects do not require a psychedelic trip: when the researchers tested tabernanthalog, a non-hallucinogenic compound that activates the same receptors, the animals received similar protection against sensory-nerve loss and pain hypersensitivity.

rss_11_1788553912.title: Nations expanding their research programmes impose sweeping penalties for malpractice
rss_11_1788553912.text:
In response to high retraction rates, India, Peru and Vietnam have introduced guidelines and disciplinary measures against research misconduct.Credit: designer491/iStock via Getty

In a bid to tighten research standards, governments and funders in countries with emerging research systems are increasingly rolling out disciplinary measures for researchers who do the wrong thing. The policies include docking bonuses, restricting access to grants and lowering the rankings of institutions linked to misconduct.

The reforms come as instances of research misconduct are on the rise worldwide. In May, for example, an audit1 of biomedical papers found that the rate of fabricated citations was 12 times greater in 2025 than in 2023. And later that month, an analysis2 of 33,000 cancer studies linked roughly 12% of them to suspected paper-mill activity.

The responsibility for cleaning up research malpractice has, for a long time, been a bottom-up affair: journal editors withdraw papers; universities investigate their staff members; and independent sleuths and organizations, such as Retraction Watch, expose what they can. Sometimes researchers will come forwards and correct the record themselves once they realize that they’ve made an error.

Retractions caused by honest mistakes are extremely stressful, say researchers

But there is a growing movement, particularly in countries with emerging research communities, to take a top-down approach. Funders and governments in some nations are increasingly restricting grants and opportunities for scientists who have been accused of research-integrity malpractice. These changes seek to cover a wide range of integrity issues, from plagiarism and falsified data to image manipulation and peer-review fraud.

Elisabeth Bik, an independent research-integrity consultant based in the the San Francisco Bay area, California, welcomes the roll-out of schemes that penalize malpractice in this way. “In order to tackle misconduct, there needs to be some type of sanction,” she says. “If there wasn’t the chance of getting a ticket, we’d all be speeding. There is fierce competition in science, and if people who cheat get better papers, then why not cheat yourself? We need to see that car being pulled over to warn other people.”

The top-down approach is needed, she says, because universities can be reluctant to sanction their own researchers, fearing that it will negatively affect their reputation. “Universities don’t do a great job in holding people accountable,” explains Bik. “It needs to be done by institutions with teeth.”

But how likely are these systems to deter dodgy science? And do they risk disincentivizing honest researchers from coming forwards and admitting to their mistakes?

Redesigning research rules

India — a nation that is rapidly rising through the ranks in the Nature Index — has initiated several measures to catch research malpractice.

The Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), one of India’s largest research funders, introduced rules in May that require applicants to disclose whether they have had a paper retracted in the past five years and explain why.

Applicants also need to testify that their grant proposals — or large parts of them — were not generated by artificial-intelligence tools. The ANRF has said that, in addition to these statements from researchers, it might use a combination of tools to screen for AI use in grant applications.

This follows an announcement last year that India’s National Institutional Ranking Framework, which publishes an official ranking of research organizations each year, will start to penalize institutions that have a large number of retracted papers, such as by giving them negative marks, affecting their total score.

The citation black market: schemes selling fake references alarm scientists

By making these changes, the Indian government is hoping to put pressure on universities to be proactive in preventing problematic research from being published in the first place, rather than responding once errors and wrongdoing are discovered, says Achal Agrawal, a data scientist based in Raipur, India. Agrawal founded India Research Watch, an online platform run by volunteers that tracks research-integrity issues.

“This feels significant because it’s the first step, and the first step is always the hardest,” says Agrawal, noting that more work is needed to ensure that there are long-term improvements in research conduct. The ANRF’s requirement that retractions be disclosed, for instance, is “just a voluntary disclosure, and it only lasts five years”, he says. Moreover, it’s not clear how the information provided by researchers will be verified. “But even just as a signal, even if they don’t implement it full-scale, I still think it’s quite significant,” he says.

Agrawal is optimistic that these measures are the beginning of a wider trend in India towards a top-down approach to research-integrity enforcement. “The ANRF is one of the biggest funding agencies in India, so this will probably have a ripple-on effect,” he says. “Institutes that want researchers to get grants will also probably be more careful when recruiting researchers.”

Ramping up

In Peru, another nation that has increased its efforts to combat research malpractice, researchers risk losing pay if they break the rules. The government announced in March that it will start docking the bonuses of researchers whose work is retracted in a bid to push back against those who engage in “acts that violate ethics and scientific integrity”.

Typically, Peruvian academics who participate in one or more research projects are eligible for monthly bonuses that range from 2,617 to 4,435 Peruvian soles (US$780 to $1,320), but those who have had one or more articles retracted in the past three years will no longer qualify.

The move follows a 2024 government investigation into alleged networks of paper mills in Peru. Percy Mayta-Tristán, vice-rector for research at the Scientific University of the South in Lima, says that the changes are needed. “We have good researchers, but we weren’t incentivizing research publication in a good way,” he says.

India to penalize universities with too many retractions

However, the system runs the risk of punishing researchers whose papers are retracted because of a genuine error or insufficient attention to methods transparency. For this reason, Bik says that she would like to see the reforms tweaked so that they differentiate between honest mistakes and wilful malpractice. “You want to encourage people who find a big error in their papers and retract it or republish it. That’s a good thing,” she says.

The Vietnamese government has also announced a framework on research integrity that will roll out a series of disciplinary actions for malpractice, including written warnings, mandatory public apologies and repayment of research funding. Violations will also be recorded on a national database.

rss_12_1788553914.title: Daily briefing: GLP-1 obesity drugs slow signs of ageing in mice
rss_12_1788553914.text:
Mice on GLP-1s also performed better on cognitive tasks than those on a calorie restricted diet . Plus, satellite images showed early warning signs of glacier collapse near the Nepal–Tibet border and the impact of people saying fewer words aloud.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

The flash flood destroyed many buildings and left villages covered in mud and debris.Credit: Arun Sankar/AFP via Getty

Satellite images taken just days before the high-altitude collapse of rock and ice that caused a catastrophic flash flood in Nepal showed concerning signs of an unstable glacier system, geophysicist Manoochehr Shirzaei tells Nature. However, such events are still difficult to predict using existing monitoring systems, he says. An effective early-warning system would need to integrate several approaches that screen glacial regions, ramp up surveillance of any that are identified as potentially unstable and model what might happen in the event of a collapse.

Nature | 5 min read

The GLP-1 medication semaglutide — sold as Wegovy for the treatment of obesity — might have anti-ageing properties, a study in mice suggests. Researchers found that older female mice taking a GLP-1 drug lived longer than did mice not taking one, and the treatment slowed several biological changes associated with ageing, such as inflammation. The treated mice also performed better at cognitive tests than did untreated mice on a strict diet, which suggests the drug has benefits that aren’t explained by calorie reduction alone, says biologist and study co-author Danica Chen.

130,000 The number of baby common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) that researchers have released into the Adriatic Sea this year. Their aim is to curb the booming population of blue crabs (Callinectes sapidus), which are muscling out other species in the Mediterranean. The octopuses will prey on the crabs — if they survive to adulthood. (Scientific American | 4 min read)

The Canadian government has announced that the nation’s universities have recruited 64 international researchers as part of a campaign to attract foreign talent. Forty-eight of these researchers are moving from the United States, taking up positions in fields ranging from health sciences to engineering. The group will receive a total of 500 million Canadian dollars (about US$360 million) in funding for eight years. Many US scientists face funding uncertainty as the administration of President Donald Trump attempts to cut research grants.

Nature | 5 min read

California blackworms (Lumbriculus variegatus) can move faster in confined spaces than they can in open ones. Researchers found that the tiny worms could zip through narrow tubes that were only around twice their width in around one minute, but took much longer to traverse wider channels — results that held true in computer models of strings of beads. The findings could inform the design of robots that squeeze through tight spaces, which could be used to slither through rubble or deliver drugs inside people’s bodies.

Features & opinion

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope was launched to map the invisible Universe, but its biggest discoveries could emerge from its use beyond this goal, argues astronomer Priyamvada Natarajan. The telescope’s data will immediately become public, enabling scientists to interrogate its findings for their own research goals, and one quarter of the instrument’s operational time will be allocated to pursuits that can deviate from its core objectives. “Transformative scientific infrastructure does more than answer the queries that justified its construction. It expands the realm of questions that can be asked at all,” Natarajan writes.

Nature | 5 min read

In a world of self-service and remote working, people are speaking fewer words aloud each day now than they were 20 years ago, and the decline is particularly pronounced in people under the age of 25. This dwindling number of spoken words could have knock-on effects, some researchers worry. Replacing speech with text-based messages bypasses some of the cognitive effort required to listen and respond to another person, and saved message histories eliminate the need to remember what’s been said — shortcuts that could cause long-lasting changes in the brain over time.

Image of the week

This cookie, called a µBite, was made from recycled plastic and food waste. Researchers used a process called oxidative hydrothermal dissolution to break down polyethylene terephthalate and crop offcuts such as corn stalks into small molecules. They then fed these molecules to engineered yeast that can convert them into an edible, 3D-printable slurry. A stint in the microwave solidifies the printout into a biscuit. The team have yet to taste their creation, but say the treats smell good enough to eat. (Science Alert | 4 min read)
